title: Durango's Horsefly History adds new elements to tunnel, ghost tours
excerpt: Local company blends town’s history with the paranormal
content:
Many of us make our way up and down downtown Durango multiple times a day. And while we may get mired in the daily routine, how many of us have stopped to think about what – and who – came before us?

And are some of those people still here, just in an otherworldy form?

For the history – and paranormal – curious, Durango’s Horsefly History Tours has added and upgraded its history and ghost tour offerings.

Horsefly History owner Laine Johnson has added a Ghost Train: Hauntings on Main Avenue tour for those who are looking for stories about hauntings of the Durango & Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad. Participants should be aware that this tour does not include a ride on the train – it does, however, begin with a ghost story about the train in front of the depot and makes it way up Main Avenue, with the group stopping at points along the route to learn about the history of the people who may – or may not – have moved into the spirit realm. And people are invited to hunt for their own spirits.

“This one is more family friendly, so people that have kids can come on this one. The stories are a little less violent, a little more of the spooky, woman in a white dress sort of stories that won’t scare people too much,” Johnson said. “They get EMF detectors for free to use on the tour and do a little ghost hunting. There are a couple of stops where we tend to get some activity.”

Participants are also shown how to use an app for ghost hunting that tour guides use that has pretty good results, she said.

Horsefly has also made its Haunted Tunnel Ghost Tour a little darker and scarier, Johnson said. Included in the tour is the story of Durango’s own Lizzie Borden.

“We have stories in that are a little more chilling,” she said. “We have a story about Ralph Ray, who was an ax murderer,” who, Horsefly’s website says, murdered his mother with a hatchet in 1891.

And then there is the tunnel – a 19th-century tunnel that once connected a saloon to a dance hall where sporting girls entertained railroad men and miners, Horsefly’s website says.

When asked to give us an example of something Johnson’s seen that she can’t quite explain, she said it’s got to be the dark figure she and others have seen in the tunnel … the one you will be going into if you take the tour.

“That’s something we weren’t expecting as far as potentially having some energies down there that might not even be human but might come from the earth itself,” she said. “A lot of places that have blocked off tunnels report dark, menacing kind of shadow figures that guard them, and this is something with the 7-foot cloaked figure.”

She said the people who work in the building above the tunnel (we’re not naming it here) have also seen the figure, as well as some of her staff members, who may have begun their paranormal tour careers as skeptics, but soon found themselves beginning to believe.

“People have seen it,” Johnson said. “I’ve even had a high schooler who was with me one day who didn’t believe in ghosts who was helping me shut the tunnel down and he screamed because he saw the shadow figure peek out from around the corner. … When I started giving the tunnel tour years ago, we had rocks thrown at us from back there where the figure is.”

The company has also accumulated a photo gallery of things that have been seen, she said – including a photograph of the shadow figure.

“We’re not sure if he was ever even human, but that’s a new photo from last year, and we show all these photos on the tour,” she said. “We just keep adding photos every year, which is so amazing and fun. And it definitely makes going in there scarier every year. So, I mean, now that there’s this cloaked figure, I haven’t been in there by myself since we got that photo.”

Something Johnson gets excited about when she begins to lead a tour is to discover Durango residents in the group.

“I’m always excited when I hear they’re locals because there’s just little things you’ve never noticed,” she said. “And even people that have lived here their whole lives always walk away with something new that they didn’t know. It’s really neat to see that transformation when people are like, ‘Oh my God, I can’t believe that happened there.’ Or this building they’ve been going to for coffee every day, it’s like, ‘Wow, I can’t believe this whole explosion happened in the basement.’”

And while the tours are fun – who doesn’t like a good scare? – Johnson said there are a couple of reasons why she continues to work as hard as she does to add to the tours. First, she’s gotten to know some of the families who are descendants of the early people she talks about. She conducts extensive research about the history of the area, and is constantly adding new information, stories and photographs to the tours. And a lot of that comes from them.

“I feel indebted to this community for the love that people and support that everybody has shown, and that they’ve entrusted me with some of these stories,” she said. “So I feel definitely a little protective over some things.”

She also enjoys seeing people on her tour have a great time and “feel so jazzed about our history,” to the point they take what they learned on the tour and gone home and gotten into the history of Durango.

“Afterwards, I’ve had people on the tours that have really done the deep dive and really gotten into the local history after coming on a tour,” she said. “I had a 90-year-old who was born and raised here, and is like third generation, and he had never seen the tunnels. He was one of the first people to come on the ghost tour, and it was so rewarding for him to see this place that he had heard so much about.

“I love history, I love ghost stories, and so it’s the best thing in the world for me that I just get to do that and dig up stories and learn new things. It really makes you feel more connected to Durango.”
